extracted.intended_audience: administrative analysts, public agency managers, and students of public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and standards for mapping, evaluating, and improving administrative sequences (the series of tasks and moves that accomplish an administrative objective) in public agencies or large organizations. Covers charting, timing, task-quality evaluation, routing, centralization vs. decentralization, and criteria for eliminating or combining steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide sequence into steps and count moves
rubrics_metrics.description: The first operation in analyzing an existing or proposed administrative sequence is to divide it into steps or individual tasks. Then it must be seen how many 'moves' are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present this information graphically (superimpose flow on organization chart or use cross-analysis/flow charts) to show number and distance of moves and to reveal back-tracking. Use the chart as an index to indicate where more investigation is likely to be fruitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion delay components
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion delay caused by any transfer consists of three elements: (a) the time required for the physical transfer of the work from one person to another, (b) the time before the recipient gets around to acting on the matter, and (c) the time it takes him to decide what he should do about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating delay, consider physical and organizational distance (e.g., inter-divisional mail may take hours or days). Use examples (memo to superior may take minutes or weeks) to quantify typical delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make administrative moves worthwhile
rubrics_metrics.description: To make any administrative move worth-while, its direct and indirect time and money costs must be compensated by (a) increased efficiency through specialization, and (b) prevention of possible costly mistakes through supervision and control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before introducing moves beyond the absolute minimum needed, ascertain whether gains from improved operation and control will outweigh probable expense and delay (consider intangible factors such as honesty and ability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize number and distance of administrative moves
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative moves should be as few and short as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct routing is essential because time and cost increase with physical and organizational distance. Keep formal signatures and clearances down to the minimum; materiel should travel as rapidly as possible between those who do the actual work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each task must contribute to the basic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Each task should contribute positively to the basic purpose. Every step should fit into a logical pattern and should have definite and essential results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the need for a step is doubtful, the presumption is in favor of eliminating it. Care should be taken that work is never duplicated, particularly in control functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine similar tasks
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining reduces the number of administrative moves and permits preliminary work (e.g., familiarization with background) to be done once instead of repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance skill, importance, and authority in tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Each task should be well-balanced: the three elements which make up the quality of a task (skill/experience required, importance of subject matter, and discretion/authority inherent) should be well adjusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not waste high skill and authority on unimportant matters, nor saddled high-judgment tasks with unessential detail. Reassign or redesign tasks where the elements are mismatched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate task quality using three questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate a task's 'quality' by answering: (1) How much skill and experience are required for performing the task? (2) How important is the subject matter; what are the consequences of omission or improper performance? (3) How much discretion, judgment, and authority are inherent in the work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferably sum up in numerical terms. Do not rate tasks by the grade or salary of those who perform them; base evaluation on aptitudes strictly necessary for the task. Use results to align tasks with positions sensibly and economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for functionality (line vs. staff) of each task
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine a task's 'functionality' — its exact place in the network of line and staff functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With flow charts and data on functions/units, use functionality to decide whether the sequence is the best way to accomplish objectives or whether it could be done more simply and economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include every move when charting sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In tracing the course of a sequence, care must be taken to include every move and not merely the principal ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify facts by actually following the sequence around; don't rely solely on written instructions or executive descriptions. Account for even the most perfunctory steps because each move introduces expense and delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cross-analysis (flow) charts correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-analysis or flow charts are graphic indexes showing brief descriptions of steps across columns and the units/officers performing them down columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They illustrate organizational distance and distinguish operating steps from control steps. Note: the chart itself does not provide a basis for concluding any step is unnecessary — it is an indicator where thorough investigation may be most fruitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement charts with timing data where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement flow charts by preparing a 'time table' showing average times between key steps if the files will yield the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing data helps quantify motion delay and identify bottlenecks; use it when available to support qualitative judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask 'why?' about every task; eliminate if no justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider each task both as an entity and in relation to the whole purpose of the sequence; particular emphasis should be placed on the question 'why?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of a definite answer from those responsible for the task indicates it may perhaps be eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple administration; guard against unnecessary formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: The best administration is simple; eliminate steps which are mere formalities or administrative fictions (e.g., excessive signing by high executives who do not read/prepare documents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, use rubber-stamping, issuing over subordinate signatures, or impersonal organizational signatures to reduce unnecessary moves and delays. Always check qualitative analysis against objective statistical and cost-accounting data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust centralization vs. devolution according to context
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no one best degree of concentration of authority; the proper adjustment depends on factors including the nature of the work, the environment (physical, political, legal, socio-psychological), the caliber of personnel, and mutual feelings/trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of pendulum swings between over-concentration (which overloads central officials) and extreme devolution (which generates duplication and conflict). Seek balance appropriate to personnel quality and organizational context.
